# Weave agent instructions

- Before adding complexity for a speculative or vanishingly unlikely race or security edge case, explain the concrete failure mode, likelihood, and complexity cost, and get buy-in. Do not silently expand scope for theoretical robustness.
- Validate unknown values once at the boundary that owns them, then pass typed values inward. Do not defensively revalidate values already guaranteed by a schema, constructor, or internal type.
- Test each behavior once at the strongest boundary that observes it. Do not add test-only exports or production code paths solely to support tests.

# Verify Weave

Weave is a read-only bridge over OpenCode sessions. `bun run serve` exposes an NDJSON watch at `POST /rpc`; the React client subscribes to it. Each `SessionFeed` contains ordered source groups. Each source owns its SSE, seeded projection, and retry budget for the process lifetime, including periods with zero viewers. The single-source fixtures use group id `local`. This skill drives the real server through the native client built from `Group` in `src/shared/rpc.ts`, with a fake only at OpenCode's HTTP and event-SSE boundary. The client feature uses `bun run dev:mock` to own that fake, real server, and Vite client.

Read `features/README.md` first. Use one feature file as the recipe for the behavior you need to prove. The commands below use the legacy single `local` source. For explicit multi-source configuration and isolation, also run [Multiple sources](features/multi-source.md).

## Launch

Run from the worktree at the SHA under test, after `bun install --frozen-lockfile`.

```sh
bun run verify launch --worktree "$PWD"
```

Launch prints `LAUNCHED run=<absolute path>`. Copy that path into `RUN` and reuse it for every later command.

```sh
RUN=<absolute path from LAUNCHED>
bun run verify doctor --run "$RUN"
```

The default run directory is a unique timestamp-and-process-id child of the native OS temp directory, under `opencode/weave-verify`. Pass `--run <abs>` to choose a known location.

Launch starts `harness/session.ts`. That process starts the controlled OpenCode fake, starts the real `bun run serve` subprocess with `WEAVE_PORT=0`, reads the actual ephemeral port from the server's `Listening on http://127.0.0.1:<port>` log line, waits for the server's one source SSE plus its paginated list and active reads with zero frontends, and writes `state.json`. Launch returns only after that source seed is complete. It does not claim the RPC surface is usable; run doctor for that.

Never point the harness at an existing user Weave, OpenCode, or Tailscale listener. The harness owns its fake, server, supervisor, and ports. It uses no default listener ports.

## Doctor

```sh
bun run verify doctor --run "$RUN"
```

Doctor is read-only. It checks:

- the supervisor and server PIDs are alive;
- the actual listener PID belongs to the owned server process tree;
- the server log names the actual ephemeral port;
- the worktree SHA still matches `state.json`, and the worktree is clean;
- exactly one source connection is open, with cumulative connections at least the startup count;
- a native typed RPC client decodes one connected `local` source group within 10 seconds, proving current source health, accepted upstream auth, and the wire schema;
- the typed watch adds no source connection, list, or active request.

It writes `doctor.json` and exits non-zero on any failed check. Doctor checks live health, so you can re-run it after a fixture change. Run it before a feature, and again after any surprising result. On an uncommitted worktree, `worktree-clean` fails by design; that is interim evidence and not a clean-SHA proof.

The snapshot `startup` scenario owns the one-time startup proof before any fixture change: one source SSE, three paginated `/api/session` reads with `archived=false` and no `parentID`, one active read, no per-session or pending read, and the 502-session startup feed with the child running and zero attention.

## Client UI

The client feature starts its own runner and browser. It does not use the run directory from `launch`.

```sh
RUN=$(mktemp -d "$TMPDIR/weave-client-ui.XXXXXX")
bun .agents/skills/verify-weave/harness/client-ui.ts --worktree "$PWD" --run "$RUN"
```

The React client is the Kreisel habitat, so this is a habitat RPC smoke, not UI
acceptance. The helper starts `bun run dev:mock`, reads its `DEV_READY` URLs, and
drives headless Chrome through live feed updates, departures, returns, specimen
selection, a built preview, actual App teardown, and source recovery.
Preview builds stay inside the run directory. Animal counts and poses come from
the development inspection hook, which the built preview must not expose.

The page at `/test/harness/scene.html` mounts the actual `App` under StrictMode
and `RegistryProvider`. The browser checks WebGPU rendering, CSS resize, model
retention, and three mount/unmount cycles. It observes native GPU device
destruction, disposal events, zeroed engine resources, removed canvases, and
stopped rendering. One RPC POST remains alive through a persistent feed consumer.
This is not a driver-memory measurement or a long-run leak test.

The helper stops only processes it started, on success and failure. It uses
`WEAVE_CHROME_PATH` when set, otherwise the macOS Chrome bundle or
`/usr/bin/chromium`. Do not point it at an existing preview, runner, OpenCode,
or Tailscale listener.

The client smoke also checks the session placard's typed context, native title
copy, folder tooltip, Escape focus return, outside close, and fixed mobile
overlay. At 390x844, opening and copying must leave canvas bounds, drawing
buffer, and camera matrices identical. Preview builds stay inside the run
directory so verification never overwrites a running production bundle.

The `specimen` scenario checks an isolated specimen pass on WebGPU, desktop
widths of 1280, 1440, and 1920, DPR changes, the target matching the aperture's
device pixels, downsampled appearance and pose against the same board frame,
continuous phase motion across a bucket boundary, live motion, selection
replacement, offscreen hiding, removal, and closed-state render work.

`--only` accepts comma-separated scenario names. A filtered run proves only the
scenarios listed in its manifest. Use a fresh run directory for each invocation.
Set `WEAVE_CHROME_PATH` when the Chrome executable is not at the macOS default
or `/usr/bin/chromium`.

## Drive

One feature run uses the long-lived instance from launch. Feature runs are serial because each resets the shared fixture with real events.

```sh
bun run verify feature snapshot --run "$RUN"
bun run verify feature live-updates-attention --run "$RUN"
bun run verify feature lifecycle --run "$RUN"
bun run verify feature rpc-errors --run "$RUN"
```

The client UI command above is a separate feature run. It starts and stops its own runner.

`rpc-errors` runs last. It proves recovery, then exhausts ten retries with failing snapshot reads and stops the fake upstream. Current and later watches retain sessions and unavailable health. Allow about three minutes for the real backoff delays. A failed feature writes evidence and stops only its owned processes.

To run the whole lifecycle without separate commands:

```sh
bun run verify all --worktree "$PWD"
```

`all` launches a fresh instance, runs doctor, drives the four server features in order, runs cleanup, and writes the final manifest. It does not start the client runner. Pass `--run <abs>` to keep the evidence at a known location.

## Evidence

Every run writes under `$RUN`:

- `manifest.json`: code SHA, worktree, commands, feature results, final result.
- `doctor.json`: readiness checks.
- `checks.json`: every behavioral check, with feature and scenario.
- `frames.jsonl`: actual typed client feeds, with feature, scenario, client, and time.
- `requests.jsonl`: actual upstream HTTP requests observed at the fake boundary. Authorization values are reduced to `basic` or `none`.
- `raw.frames.jsonl`: raw NDJSON status, content type, and response frames for each direct protocol probe.
- `direct/*.json`: direct typed client results and failed subprocess results, one file per scenario.
- `scenarios/*.json`: one result per scenario, including its checks and request paths.
- `server.stdout.log`, `server.stderr.log`, `supervisor.json`: process logs and shutdown state.
- `cleanup.json`, `post-cleanup.json`: teardown checks and a post-teardown readability check of the evidence.

A client UI run writes `manifest.json`, `checks.json`, `screenshots/*.png`,
`dev-mock-*.log`, `dev-mock.json`, `cleanup.json`, and `post-cleanup.json` under
its own run directory. Pass means the browser observed the real feed, one
idle-to-running update, the built preview, actual App WebGPU teardown, and the
source recovery, not only that the page loaded.

Pass means a behavioral check observed the result on the real server or the real typed client. A feed is complete, so a removed session is proved by absence from the latest feed. Do not replace a failed journey with a helper-level assertion. Mocks exist only at the OpenCode public HTTP and event-SSE boundary. The process keeps temporary in-memory projections; there is no database, replay log, polling loop, startup request scan, cursor resume token, or pending-request hydration.

## Cleanup

```sh
bun run verify cleanup --run "$RUN"
```

Cleanup sends SIGTERM to the owned server and records its exit code, listener state, cumulative source connections, and open source connections. It accepts the native Bun exit 0 or 130 and requires no open source connection and no connection added during shutdown. When `rpc-errors` already closed the source, this observes the absence, not a SIGTERM cause; the unit test owns the Effect SSE scope closure. It then stops the supervisor and fake, checks the owned PIDs and both ports are gone, and writes `cleanup.json`. Finally it verifies the evidence still exists and is readable, then writes `post-cleanup.json`.

Cleanup requires base launch/doctor logs and the scenario files named by recorded feature checks. Direct RPC result files are required only when `rpc-errors` ran. A launch/doctor/cleanup run with no features needs no RPC-error files. Any failed recorded feature or unreadable required file keeps the final result at `FAIL`.

Cleanup never deletes evidence. It never kills by process name or by broad port ownership. It kills only the supervisor PID, the server runner PID, and a listener PID recorded as the runner or listener in `state.json`.

## Helpers

All helpers live in this skill directory:

- `harness/verify.ts` is the command above.
- `harness/session.ts` owns the fake, the real `bun run serve` child, and the control server. It waits for the startup seed before reporting ready. Its `POST /sessions` reset emits child-first delete events and parent-first create events; `reset: false` writes the fixture without publishing an event for the next explicit public event.
- `harness/client.ts` imports the production `Group` and builds the native client with `RpcClient.make(Group)`, `RpcClient.layerProtocolHttp`, `RpcSerialization.layerNdjson`, and `FetchHttpClient.layer` inside `Effect.scoped`. Its watcher collects complete `SessionFeed` values.
- `harness/scenarios.ts` holds the four feature runners.
- `harness/support.ts` holds evidence, control, process, and port helpers.
- `harness/client-ui.ts` starts `bun run dev:mock`, drives headless Chrome through the habitat smoke with source recovery, and writes the client evidence.

The upstream fixture reuses `test/support/fake-opencode.ts` through an import. The fixture can change sessions, active ids, events, and stream lifetime through the control server. It has no Weave test endpoint. `FakeEvents.open()` reports the active SSE controller count; `connections()` stays cumulative.

## Limits

This is a controlled-boundary proof, not a real user integration. It uses an OpenCode fake at the external HTTP and SSE boundary. It does not install OpenCode, start a real OpenCode server, or send model or provider requests. The separate real OpenCode compatibility probe is not part of this skill or its feature map.

The client feature drives headless Chrome against its controlled runner and the
built preview of the same worktree, not a user's preview. Chrome enables WebGPU.
Checks cover identity, typed state, palette phases, isolated specimen appearance,
mobile overlay geometry, actual App teardown, and bounded selected and closed
700-animal submission samples. They do not establish visual acceptance, a
production performance comparison, driver-memory recovery, or a long-run GPU
leak result.

This skill does not claim CI coverage; the repository has no CI configured.

# Weave

Weave turns your OpenCode sessions into a tank of jellies. Leave it on a spare
screen and you can see which agents are working, which are idle, and which are
waiting for you, without opening a session list.

![A dark round tank with six moon, fried-egg, and white-spotted jellies](docs/images/weave-tank.webp)

_One jelly is one session._

Weave is read-only. It watches your sessions and never sends commands to OpenCode.

## How to read the tank

Every unarchived root session and its subagents become jellies. Archiving a root
hides the whole family. A root session is slightly larger than its own subagents.
A session that remains on screen keeps its place. New sessions fade in, and
sessions that leave fade out.

Each server gets a species in the order you list your servers, cycling through
moon, fried egg, and white-spotted. Connect a laptop, a remote machine, and a
shared server, and the tank shows which sessions come from each one.

A running session is a little brighter. A pending permission glows coral. A
pending question glows amber. An OpenCode outage leaves the jellies already on
screen while Weave tries to reconnect. If it cannot reconnect, restart Weave.

![A selected white-spotted jelly beside its specimen placard with a live close-up, title, source, directory, and status](docs/images/weave-inspect.webp)

_Select a jelly to read its session details and see a live close-up._

Hover or focus a jelly to see its title. Click, tap, or press Enter to open the
placard. Its close-up shows the selected jelly live, and a faint line follows the
jelly to the placard. The title is a button. It copies a text summary of the
session, including the title, source, status, and directory. Escape or a click
on empty water closes the placard. On a phone, the placard becomes a fixed bottom
sheet.

![A coral fried-egg jelly among six jellies, marking a session waiting for permission](docs/images/weave-attention.webp)

## Watch more than one server

Weave connects to one or more OpenCode servers. It reconnects to each server
independently, so an unavailable server does not hide the others. The top-left
status icon is green when every server is connected. It is amber while a server
is connecting or retrying, and red when a server is unavailable. Click or tap it
to see the server names. If the browser loses its connection to Weave, the status
list disappears and a notice asks you to refresh the page.

## Get started

You need Bun 1.4.4 or newer and a reachable OpenCode server.

```sh
bun install
```

Start the server with the URL and password of your OpenCode server:

```sh
WEAVE_OPENCODE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4096 \
WEAVE_OPENCODE_PASSWORD=your-password \
bun run serve
```

Start the client in another terminal:

```sh
bun run dev
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173`. The client proxies `/rpc` to
`WEAVE_DEV_RPC_URL`, which defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:4310`. If you change
`WEAVE_PORT`, set `WEAVE_DEV_RPC_URL` to match.

## Configuration

| Variable                  | Required | Default     | Meaning                                |
| ------------------------- | -------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `WEAVE_OPENCODE_SOURCES`  | no       | none        | Ordered JSON array of OpenCode sources |
| `WEAVE_OPENCODE_URL`      | fallback | none        | URL of the OpenCode server             |
| `WEAVE_OPENCODE_PASSWORD` | fallback | none        | OpenCode password                      |
| `WEAVE_HOST`              | no       | `127.0.0.1` | Host the server listens on             |
| `WEAVE_PORT`              | no       | `4310`      | Port the server listens on             |

For more than one server, set `WEAVE_OPENCODE_SOURCES`:

```sh
WEAVE_OPENCODE_SOURCES='[{"id":"laptop","username":"opencode","password":"replace-laptop-password","url":"http://127.0.0.1:4096"},{"id":"remote","username":"remote-user","password":"replace-remote-password","url":"https://opencode.example.com"}]' \
bun run serve
```

Each entry needs a unique `id`, a `username`, a `password`, and an HTTP or HTTPS
`url`. The array must not be empty. Credentials stay on the backend and never
reach the browser.

When `WEAVE_OPENCODE_SOURCES` is set, it overrides `WEAVE_OPENCODE_URL` and
`WEAVE_OPENCODE_PASSWORD`. Without it, those two variables configure one server
with ID `local`. Invalid configuration stops startup. Restart Weave after a
configuration change.

## How it runs

A Bun server reads sessions from your OpenCode servers. A React client draws the
tank with Three.js from one shared live connection.

The tank shows no visible session list, dashboard, or navigation at rest. The
water makes one orbit in about eight minutes. Jellies pass through one another.
The glass is the only boundary.

## Development

To work on the tank without a real OpenCode server, run:

```sh
bun run dev:mock
```

This starts a fake OpenCode, the Weave server, and the client. It prints
`DEV_READY` with the UI URL and a control URL for switching fixtures, including a
session that leaves and returns.

Other commands:

- `bun run check` runs typecheck, lint, format check, and tests.
- `bun run build` writes the client build to `dist/client`.
- `bun run preview` serves that build and proxies `/rpc` to the same server URL as `dev`.
- `bun run verify` runs the RPC and browser checks in `.agents/skills/verify-weave`.
- `bun run format` formats the repository.

# Weave verification map

This directory is the maintained source for verifying the user-facing behavior of the Weave session-watch RPC bridge and its React client. Read this index before driving, then use the matching feature file as the recipe.

## Baseline preconditions

- Run from the Weave worktree at the SHA you intend to prove. `git rev-parse HEAD` must match the `codeSHA` in the run manifest.
- Install exactly once per clean worktree with `bun install --frozen-lockfile`. Use Bun 1.4.4 or newer.
- Start a fresh owned run with `bun run verify launch --worktree "$PWD"`. Use the absolute path it prints as `RUN` for later commands. A `--run` path must be absolute.
- Launch returns only after the server has opened one source SSE, drained the paginated unarchived list, and read the active map with zero frontends.
- Run `bun run verify doctor --run "$RUN"` and require every implementation check to pass before driving. On an uncommitted worktree, `worktree-clean` fails by design and the run is interim evidence, not a clean-SHA proof.
- Never drive a Weave, OpenCode, or Tailscale listener that this run did not start.
- Never use ports 4399 through 4403. The harness asks the real server for port 0 and records the actual ephemeral port in `state.json`.

## Driving conventions

- Treat every command as literal. Keep quoted paths unchanged.
- Drive features in order: `snapshot`, `live-updates-attention`, `lifecycle`, then `rpc-errors`.
- One long-lived server serves the whole run. The projection is owned by the serve layer and starts before the first client.
- `rpc-errors` runs last because it exhausts source retries and stops its fake upstream.
- Client UI runs use `bun .agents/skills/verify-weave/harness/client-ui.ts`. It is a habitat smoke for the development client and built preview. It starts and stops its own `bun run dev:mock` runner and headless Chrome. Do not point it at a preview or runner it did not start.
- Use the native typed RPC client built from the production `Group`. Do not add a test-only endpoint to Weave. The watch stream yields a `SessionFeed`, a list of source groups. The single-source regression fixture uses source ID `local`.
- A feed is complete. Presence and absence in the latest feed are the only truth about the collection.
- Change the upstream fixture only through `harness/session.ts` control requests. A reset emits child-first `session.deleted` and parent-first `session.created` events; a mid-scenario write uses `reset: false` and is followed by the public event under test. Writing the fixture alone does not change an already-running projection.
- The fixtures are replayable. Each control request sets deterministic sessions and publishes public events through the fake's HTTP and SSE boundary. Reproducibility comes from the fixture and the event sequence, not a product replay command.
- On a failed feature, inspect `scenarios/*.json`, `frames.jsonl`, `raw.frames.jsonl`, and `requests.jsonl` before rerunning. Cleanup already stopped owned processes; evidence stays.

## Proof and skip reporting

- Capture the user action and the resulting feed or process result, not only a final summary.
- RPC proof includes the actual typed client feed in `frames.jsonl` and the upstream request path in `requests.jsonl`.
- Error proof includes the direct client result in `direct/*.json` and the raw HTTP status, content type, and frames in `raw.frames.jsonl`.
- Lifecycle proof uses the fake's cumulative connection count and its open SSE controller count. A watch leaves both unchanged. Only backend layer close sets the open count to zero.
- Process proof includes the owned PID, actual port, and listener ownership check.
- Report an unreachable path with the attempted command and the unmet precondition. Do not report a skipped entry point as verified through a different path.
- A check that can only be made inside the harness is insufficient. Assert the observable feed, request, process result, exit code, PID, or port.

## Feature entry contract

Each feature file starts with an H1 title and one paragraph describing the user-visible behavior. It then uses exactly four H2 sections in this order.

1. `Sub-features` lists short IDs with one line for each behavior.
2. `How to get to it (user POV)` lists every user entry point.
3. `Driving it with verify-weave` starts with `Preconditions:` and pairs each user action with an exact command and observable result.
4. `Gotchas` lists traps that can waste or invalidate a run.

Keep implementation details out of the map. Name only user paths, stable handles, required state, commands, and observable proof.

## Features

- [Snapshot](./snapshot.md) covers the startup whole feed with zero frontends, paginated seed, all idle and running descendants, zero attention, whole replacement, and a watch that adds no source reads.
- [Live updates and attention](./live-updates-attention.md) covers complete feed replacement, idle retention, own permission and question counts, cross-kind ids, root archive and whole-family unarchive, individual delete, and retention across zero viewers.
- [Stream lifecycle](./lifecycle.md) covers one startup source, watch with no reads, late-viewer retention, shared projection, last cancel keeping the source, and SIGTERM teardown. Source recovery is covered in `rpc-errors`.
- [Source recovery and RPC errors](./rpc-errors.md) covers retained source health, fresh reseeding, bounded retries, zero-viewer recovery, raw NDJSON, closed transport, missing credentials, and secret-free evidence.
- [Multiple sources](./multi-source.md) covers ordered explicit configuration, independent authenticated HTTP and SSE sources, colliding IDs, blocked startup, source-local recovery, and sibling flow after retry exhaustion.
- [Client habitat UI (browser smoke)](./client-sessions-ui.md) checks the real feed, session updates, departure and return, debug SPS behavior, built preview, App teardown, retention through source recovery, and the top-left connection HUD. Its source-controls scenario checks one source disclosure, the terminal unavailable precedence, persistent problem text, mobile sheet clearance, live health updates, and the transport-loss notice. # Client habitat UI

The client is the Kreisel habitat: one WebGPU tank, one school of three
server-derived jelly species, one shared RPC subscription. A session is an animal, keyed by source plus
session id. Roots are larger than their own children. The page has no session
list, dashboard or navigation at rest. A small top-left HUD keeps the FPS
readout and a source disclosure icon. A persistent status notice appears only
when the browser stream is lost or a source is retrying or unavailable. Hover or
focus shows a bare
title; deliberate selection opens one fixed-width specimen placard. Its desktop
window renders the selected animal through an isolated specimen camera.
A debug query expands the readout with SPS and mean frame interval.

This feature is a browser smoke over the same controlled feed. It proves the
real feed becomes one animal per unarchived session, a live status change
updates the same animal without resetting the school, a replacement feed
departs only absent keys, the built preview mounts the habitat, the FPS
readout uses a closed wall-clock sample and detailed stats require a debug query,
one development page checks actual App WebGPU teardown,
and upstream recovery keeps the last school without a transport notice.

## Gotchas

- The owned Chrome profile treats only its fixture UI origin as secure so the
  clipboard API works on the runner's HTTP Tailscale address. Focus emulation
  makes headless `:focus` match a focused browser window. Native Enter dispatch
  includes the carriage-return text, and Escape includes its virtual key code.

- `dev:mock` binds Vite to `WEAVE_DEV_HOST` when set, otherwise to the Tailscale
  IPv4 address when `tailscale ip -4` returns one, and to `127.0.0.1` otherwise.
  The client helper sets `WEAVE_DEV_HOST=127.0.0.1` so its temporary runner never
  listens on the tailnet. Read the URL from `DEV_READY`; do not assume port 5173.
- The runner uses ephemeral ports for Vite, control, server, and fake. Never
  point it at a user preview, OpenCode, or Tailscale listener.
- Case changes are serial. Each session-changing case resets the fixture with
  real delete and create events before it applies its own events. A single
  replacement feed is reconciled by identity, so a reset that returns every key
  cancels the in-progress departure instead of rebuilding the school.
- `disconnect` ends the fake's current SSE stream, not the fake process. The
  backend reconnects automatically. Its source icon updates independently of the
  browser transport notice.
- The main runner stays on one source instance. The source-controls scenario owns
  a separate four-source runner and stops all of its ports after the scenario.
- The habitat exposes `window.__weaveHabitat` only under Vite development. The
  harness reads animal counts, poses, the backend, and draw calls from it. The
  production preview must not expose it, and the helper asserts that.
- The habitat prepares the initial feed's normal and specimen rendering paths
  before starting its animation loop. An empty initial feed is valid. Closing
  releases the specimen target textures but retains its pipeline until unmount.
  Three reopens must restore the same texture counts. A closed frame submits the
  board default and OIT accumulation passes plus its resolve. Selection adds
  specimen default/accumulation passes, its resolve, and the aperture overlay.
  Later feed changes can introduce material or geometry variants that were not
  present during preparation.
- The FPS readout refreshes every 500 ms. Detailed stats are query-gated, not
  environment-gated. The detailed counter works in the
  production build and shows only SPS, FPS, and mean frame interval from the
  last closed wall-clock sample. SPS counts completed fixed steps, so it can
  stay near 60 while FPS falls when rendering is the bottleneck; it does not
  measure GPU memory and cannot prove or disprove a leak.
- The page owns one `watchSessions` atom subscription. `Atom.keepAlive` keeps it
  alive after the last consumer unmounts, so the page issues one RPC POST and
  later mounts reuse it. The ROOT backend source connection stays on for the
  process lifetime. The renderer never opens a second RPC or SDK subscription.
- The lifecycle page uses the actual App and renderer. Native device destruction
  is not a driver-memory measurement or a long-run leak test. The page does not
  establish visual acceptance.
- The helper kills only the processes it started. Leave an intentionally
  running preview alone.

# Stream lifecycle

The serve layer owns the OpenCode event stream and projection. It connects and seeds before any viewer, then keeps publishing with zero viewers. Viewers read the retained feed without opening a source. A normal SIGTERM closes the layer and listener. Source recovery and retry exhaustion are proved in [Source recovery and RPC errors](./rpc-errors.md). That feature closes the source before cleanup, so cleanup observes source absence rather than proving SIGTERM closed a live SSE. The layer-scope test in `test/session-watch.test.ts` proves live SSE closure.

## Sub-features

- `lifecycle-startup-zero-frontend` starts one source SSE and one seed with zero viewers before any RPC client connects.
- `lifecycle-watch-no-reads` attaches a viewer without a new source connection, list read, or active read.
- `lifecycle-late-viewer-retains` keeps the process projection and observed attention while zero viewers are connected, then serves both to a later viewer.
- `lifecycle-two-frontends-shared` serves two viewers from one source and one projection; cancelling one leaves the other receiving events.
- `lifecycle-sigterm-teardown` sends SIGTERM and proves the server listener closes, then observes that no source connection remains open and no replacement opened.
- `lifecycle-source-recovery` is covered by `rpc-errors/source-recovery` and `rpc-errors/source-exhaustion`.

## How to get to it (user POV)

- Start the bridge with `bun run serve`. It opens its OpenCode source before any browser or RPC client connects.
- Connect one watch subscription. It receives the current feed.
- Open a second watch subscription at the same time. Both receive the same projection.
- Cancel one subscription. Keep watching with the other.
- Cancel the last subscription. The source stays open and the projection keeps updating.
- Connect again. The new viewer receives everything observed while it was gone.
- Stop the server with SIGTERM. The process closes its source connection, exits with the native signal code, and releases its port.
- Drop the upstream event stream. Watches retain sessions and report source health while the backend retries.

## Gotchas

- Attention is retained across viewers. A new subscription does not reset it. Startup and recovery snapshots start attention at zero.
- The fake connection counter is cumulative. `openConnections` is the live controller count. A watch must leave both unchanged.
- Two concurrent viewers share one source and one projection. Expect one connection for both, not two.
- Cancelling one viewer must not close the source. Cancelling the last viewer must not close it either. Only the serve-layer scope close aborts it.
- Upstream failure changes source health, not RPC watch liveness. After ten failed retries, restart the backend to retry again.
- SIGTERM may exit with 0 or the native Bun signal code 130. Both are successful intentional shutdown. Do not mark 130 as a verification failure.
- Keep retry exhaustion in `rpc-errors` so earlier features run against a connected source.

# Live updates and attention

The process-owned projection publishes a new complete `SessionFeed` on every change. Metadata, activity, status, outcome, and request events replace the prior feed. Optional fields that disappear upstream disappear from the next feed; they do not linger. Attention is own-only on every session and is counted from the server's one upstream connection, so it survives with zero viewers. Idle children stay in the collection.

## Sub-features

- `live-records` renames, moves, records a viewed activity, records a failed outcome, then clears the optional title, outcome, and viewed fields from a complete feed.
- `live-running-idle-retained` updates an idle child to running and back to idle while keeping it in the collection.
- `live-attention-permission-own` counts a permission id on its owning session only. Unknown replies do nothing; a reply clears the owner's count.
- `live-attention-question-own` counts a question form id on its owning session only. Unknown cancels do nothing; reply and cancel clear the owner's count.
- `live-attention-cross-kind` tracks permission and question requests independently on the same session.
- `live-root-archive` removes an archived root and its family, forgets pending requests, and restores the whole family with fresh zero attention on unarchive.
- `live-delete-individual` removes each deleted session on its own child-first delete event, without removing its parent or child.
- `live-shared-retention` keeps observed attention while zero viewers are connected and serves it to a later viewer.

## How to get to it (user POV)

- Keep the bridge running. The projection is already live before any viewer connects.
- In OpenCode, rename or move a session, change its outcome, or open it. The bridge publishes a complete feed with the updated session.
- Start or finish a child session. Its status changes and it stays in the collection.
- Trigger a permission request or a question form on any session. Only the owning session's count changes, even if no browser is open.
- Reply to or cancel a request. The owner's count clears.
- Archive a root or delete sessions. The archived family leaves and its tracked state is forgotten. Each deleted session leaves on its own delete event.
- Attach a viewer later. It receives the current feed, including attention observed while it was absent.

## Driving it with verify-weave

Preconditions:

- The run was launched from the worktree under test and doctor passed every implementation check.
- The upstream fake is still running. Do not run `rpc-errors` before this feature; `rpc-errors` ends the upstream last.
- Start each scenario from its own fixture. `controlSessions` resets the projection with child-first delete events and parent-first create events. A mid-scenario fixture write uses `reset: false` and is followed by the exact public event under test.

- **Complete records.** Run `bun run verify feature live-updates-attention --run "$RUN"`. The `records` scenario changes title, directory, viewed time, and outcome, then removes optional fields. Each complete feed keeps id, time, location, status, and attention without retaining omitted fields.
- **Idle retention.** The `running-idle-retained` scenario starts with a visible idle child. After `session.execution.started`, the child is running with its parent id. After `session.execution.succeeded`, the child is idle and still present.
- **Permission attention.** The `attention-own` scenario asks permission `per_child` on the child. The child reaches `permissions: 1`; the root and deep child stay at `0`. A request on the root reaches `1` on the root only. Unknown replies emit no feed: the `unknown-reply-no-feed` check uses a metadata barrier and requires exactly one new feed. Replying to `per_child` drops the child to `0` and leaves the root at `1`.
- **Question attention.** The same scenario creates question `frm_child` on the child and `frm_deep` on the deep child. Each owner reaches `questions: 1`; the root stays at `0`. An unknown cancel changes nothing. Replying to `frm_child` drops only the child to `0` while the deep child stays at `1`. Cancelling `frm_deep` then drops the deep child to `0`. The child permission stays at `1` through both.
- **Cross-kind ids.** The `attention-cross-kind` scenario creates permission `per_shared` and question `frm_shared` on one child. The child reports one of each. Replying to the permission clears only the permission.
- **Root archive.** The `root-archive` scenario asks a permission on the child, then archives the root. The root, child, and deep child leave the feed. Unarchive re-reads the list and active map and returns the family with zero attention. This fixture's active map is empty, so its sessions return idle. A late reply for the old request emits no feed, proved with a one-feed barrier. A new child request counts only on the child.
- **Delete.** The `delete-individual` scenario sends child-first `session.deleted` events for a deep child, its child, and the root. Each event removes only its own session. The parent stays until its own event.
- **Retention across zero viewers.** The [lifecycle](./lifecycle.md) `late-viewer-retains` scenario proves last-cancel source retention and attention updates with no viewers.
- **Proof.** Inspect `frames.jsonl` for the named ids and counts, `scenarios/attention-own.json` for the unknown-reply barrier and the check list, and `scenarios/records.json` for the optional-field checks.

## Gotchas

- Attention is own-only. A child request never changes the root count.
- There is no family count, no root aura, and no rollup footnote.
- Attention is process-owned. It survives with zero viewers and is retained for later viewers. Do not assert zero attention for a new subscription.
- Permission and form events are live and ephemeral. OpenCode mints each id once and rejects a duplicate pending id, so do not build fixtures that send the same id twice.
- A reply or cancel for an id the connection never observed must do nothing.
- Full feeds replace optional fields. If an upstream summary has no title or outcome, the next feed omits it.
- A failed or succeeded execution event returns the session to idle. An idle child stays in the whole collection.
- Archiving a root removes the whole family and forgets pending requests, including ones observed before the archive. Child archive is not a supported event.
- Unarchive re-reads the global unarchived list plus the active map. The whole family returns with its own counts at zero; pending requests on other sessions are retained.
- Deleting a session removes only that session. Delete events arrive child-first; each event removes its own record.
- Pending ids are keyed by request kind and id, with the owning session stored as the value. This scenario checks independent permission and question counts, not a same-string cross-kind collision.
- Scenario resets clear old families with real delete events. Do not rely on writing the fixture alone.

# Multiple sources

Weave accepts an ordered explicit source list. Each server has its own credentials, session state, attention requests, health, and retry budget. An unavailable source leaves sibling feeds live.

## Sub-features

- `configuration`: authoritative JSON configuration, stable unique IDs, input order, HTTP or HTTPS URLs, safe errors, and legacy fallback.
- `independence`: a blocked first seed permits the second source to publish.
- `collisions`: identical session, parent, permission, and question IDs stay source-local.
- `recovery`: only the dropped source is replaced by a fresh snapshot. Siblings continue during backoff and after exhaustion.
- `secrets`: raw feed and server logs exclude source usernames, passwords, and authorization values.

## How to get to it (user POV)

Set `WEAVE_OPENCODE_SOURCES` before `bun run serve`, then subscribe to `/rpc`. Each array entry requires `id`, `username`, `password`, and `url`. See the root README for a placeholder example.

## Driving it with verify-weave

Preconditions: use the worktree and SHA under review, install with `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, and keep the worktree clean for final evidence.

Run `bun .agents/skills/verify-weave/harness/multi-source.ts --run <absolute-new-directory>` from that worktree. The runner starts two independently controlled HTTP and SSE fakes with distinct Basic credentials and the real server on ephemeral ports. It blocks the first seed, observes the healthy second feed, releases the seed, sends colliding requests, drops and recovers the first source, and exhausts that source while the sibling stays live. Allow about four minutes.

Require `result: "PASS"` in `manifest.json` and `pass: true` in every `checks.json` entry. Inspect `frames.jsonl`, `raw.frames.json`, scrubbed `requests.jsonl`, both server logs, and `cleanup.json`. Cleanup must show closed fake and server ports and server exit 0 or 130.

Run `bun run check` for invalid configuration and legacy fallback cases, plus virtual-clock recovery and initial-group tests. Run `bun run verify all --worktree "$PWD"` for the single-source regression map. Run the existing client habitat smoke after fixture changes.

## Gotchas

- This runner owns its processes and cleans them up on success or failure. It never drives an existing listener.
- The two-source runner is separate from the single-source `verify all` fixture. Neither runner requires evidence from the other; run both for full server coverage.
- The runner records the SHA and whether the worktree was clean. Dirty-worktree evidence is interim evidence.
- Pending requests are not hydrated during startup or recovery. A fresh source starts with zero attention.
- Source health icons and details are verified by [Client habitat UI](./client-sessions-ui.md).

# Source recovery and RPC errors

Upstream failures change the required `health` on the `local` source group. They do not fail the watch. The last sessions remain visible during retries and after exhaustion. RPC transport failures remain separate failures.

## Sub-features

- `rpc-direct-feed` decodes the production `SessionFeed` through the native client.
- `rpc-raw-chunk` checks HTTP 200, NDJSON, and a raw `Chunk` frame.
- `source-recovery` observes reconnecting health, retained sessions, a fresh replacement snapshot, and a reset retry budget after successful seeding.
- `source-zero-viewers` recovers while no viewers are attached.
- `source-exhaustion` fails every reconnect seed, closes each attempt SSE, stops after ten retries, and serves retained unavailable feeds to current and later watches.
- `rpc-closed-transport` fails a native client without a feed and records the actual error tag and cause.
- `rpc-missing-credentials` exits non-zero and names the missing configuration key.
- `rpc-no-secrets` scans evidence written so far for controlled credentials. Cleanup performs the final scan.

## How to get to it (user POV)

- Connect a watch to the bridge. The feed includes source health.
- End the upstream SSE. The source reports `reconnecting` with the retry number and delay, while retaining its sessions.
- Restore upstream access. A new SSE opens before the bridge reads a fresh snapshot. The source reports `connected` and replaces old sessions.
- Keep the upstream unavailable through ten retries. The source reports `unavailable`; watches stay open. A later watch receives the same retained feed. Restart the bridge to retry after exhaustion.
- Connect to a closed RPC port. The native client fails without a feed.
- Start without credentials. The process exits and names the missing key.

## Driving it with verify-weave

Preconditions:

- Launch an owned run from the SHA under test and pass doctor.
- A fresh launched run with passing doctor is sufficient. On a shared full run, run this feature last, after `snapshot`, `live-updates-attention`, and `lifecycle`.
- Allow about three minutes for the real retry delays. The harness does not shorten production timing.

Run `bun run verify feature rpc-errors --run "$RUN"`.

The `source-recovery` scenario drops SSE, changes the fixture without events during the outage, and requires a fresh connected snapshot. It drops again and requires retry `1`, then closes all viewers during recovery.

The `source-exhaustion` scenario makes snapshot HTTP reads return 503 after SSE connects. It requires exactly ten new connections, zero open connections after exhaustion, retained sessions, and live current and later watches. The raw response must still be a `Chunk`, not an upstream-error `Exit`. Restoring snapshot access must not restart an exhausted source.

The other scenarios retain native closed-transport, missing-credential, raw NDJSON, and secret-redaction checks. Evidence is in `scenarios/source-recovery.json`, `scenarios/source-exhaustion.json`, `frames.jsonl`, `requests.jsonl`, `raw.frames.jsonl`, `direct/closed-transport.json`, and `checks.json`.

Deterministic service-boundary tests in `test/source-recovery.test.ts` prove eleven total attempts for startup connection and seed failures, the exact delay sequence, and closure of failed seed scopes. Run them with `bun run test test/source-recovery.test.ts`.

## Gotchas

- The fake's `events.end()` closes current SSE connections but accepts new ones. It proves recovery, not exhaustion.
- Acknowledging SSE alone does not reset the budget. The seed must also succeed.
- Each recovery starts a fresh projection. Pending attention hydration remains deferred, so recovered sessions start with zero attention.
- Run this feature last because it leaves the source exhausted and stops its fake upstream.
- Doctor accepts a recovered source when it has one open connection and a connected typed feed. It fails while the source is reconnecting or exhausted.
- Cleanup compares cumulative connections with the count immediately before shutdown, not the initial count.
- A source outage is not an RPC transport failure. Keep the closed-port check separate.

# Snapshot

The server builds one projection when the process starts, before any client connects. It subscribes to OpenCode events, waits for `server.connected`, drains the unarchived collection at `archived=false` with no `parentID` filter, and reads the active ids. The seeded `SessionFeed` has one `local` source group and zero attention. Before seeding completes, a viewer can receive an empty group with `connecting` health. Every child under an unarchived root is included, idle or running, at any depth.

## Sub-features

- `snapshot-startup-first-feed` publishes one `local` source group from the 502-session startup fixture before any reset, with the running child and zero attention.
- `snapshot-startup-pagination` reads the mixed collection across more than one page at server start, with one active read and no per-session fanout.
- `snapshot-all-children` includes idle and running descendants at any depth under an unarchived root.
- `snapshot-zero-attention` starts every returned permission and question count at zero.
- `snapshot-full-replace` publishes the current whole collection after a fixture reset, not a patch of an older one.
- `snapshot-watch-no-reads` attaches a viewer without another source connection, list read, or active read.
- `snapshot-no-pending-reads` keeps permission and form endpoints out of the seed.

## How to get to it (user POV)

- Start the bridge with `bun run serve`. The projector starts with the process, before any viewer.
- Connect a watch subscription with the native RPC client built from `Group` in `src/shared/rpc.ts`. The first item is the current feed.
- Open another viewer. It replays the same current feed.
- Change the collection upstream. The next feed is the whole collection again.

## Driving it with verify-weave

Preconditions:

- The run was launched from the worktree under test with `bun run verify launch --worktree "$PWD" --run "$RUN"`. Launch waits for one source SSE, the paginated list seed, and one active read with zero frontends. The startup fixture takes three list requests.
- `bun run verify doctor --run "$RUN"` passed every implementation check. On an uncommitted worktree the `worktree-clean` check fails by design. Doctor checks live health, so you can re-run it after a fixture change.
- Fixture resets go through `harness/session.ts`: child-first deletes, parent-first creates, then execution-started events for active sessions. Scenarios emit archive, unarchive, and metadata events separately. Viewers never trigger seeding; startup, unarchive, and source recovery do.

- **Startup first feed.** Run `bun run verify feature snapshot --run "$RUN"` before any other feature. Its `startup` scenario records one source connection and one source stream, the paginated seed below, one active read, and no per-session or pending read. The typed client decodes one `local` group with the 502-session startup fixture, the child running, and zero attention before any fixture reset.
- **Startup pagination.** The same scenario reads three `/api/session` pages with `limit=500&archived=false`, no `parentID`, one `/api/session/active`, and no individual `/api/session/<id>` read. The startup fixture has 501 roots plus one running child, so 500 is a page size and not a cap.
- **All children.** The `all-children` scenario sets a visible root with idle and running children, an idle intermediate with an idle grandchild, a running grandchild under that intermediate, an archived root with a child, and a session whose parent does not exist. The feed contains every unarchived-family id, including the idle intermediate and idle deep child. It omits the archived pair and the outside-family session.
- **Zero attention.** The `first-feed` scenario requires every returned attention object to be `{ permissions: 0, questions: 0 }`. The lifecycle `late-viewer-retains` scenario proves attention observed later stays with the process and is not reset per viewer.
- **Full replacement.** The `full-replace` scenario publishes `ses_before`, then resets the fixture to `ses_after` through delete and create events. The next feed contains `ses_after` and not `ses_before`.
- **Watch adds no reads.** `doctor` records `watch-adds-no-source-requests`; the lifecycle `startup-zero-frontend` scenario records `watch-start-same-source-connection` and `watch-start-no-source-requests`.
- **No pending reads.** The `no-pending-reads` scenario requires every request path in the seed and reset to avoid `permission` and `form`.
- **Proof.** Use `doctor.json`, `scenarios/startup.json`, `scenarios/first-feed.json`, `scenarios/whole-collection.json`, `scenarios/all-children.json`, `frames.jsonl`, and `requests.jsonl`.

## Gotchas

- The first stream item is the feed. Do not scan for a `connected` or `sessions` event type.
- A feed is complete. Absence of an id means the session is not in the collection.
- 500 is a page size, not a total cap. Pagination follows the next cursor until it is absent or a page is empty. The startup fixture seeds 502 sessions before the first viewer.
- Startup, unarchive, and source recovery can read multiple pages. Attaching a viewer never triggers a list or active read.
- The whole collection includes idle children at any depth. Do not treat idle or hidden parents as a visibility filter.
- Archived roots and their descendants are outside the collection. A session whose parent is missing is also outside it.
- A fixture reset must emit real delete and create events. Writing `setSessions` alone does not change an already-running projection.
- Startup attention is zero. Attention observed after startup is retained for later viewers; it is not reset by a new subscription.
- Use the native typed client for every feed. The harness does not run a CLI.

## Size the canvas in CSS

The caller sizes the canvas with CSS. The hook reads `clientWidth` and
`clientHeight` and calls `renderer.setSize(width, height, false)`, which sets the
drawing buffer and never writes CSS. A canvas with zero CSS size renders
nothing, and the hook has no fallback size.

## What the dev probe proves

- The actual habitat reports WebGPU and completed render calls.
- One CSS resize from 640 to 448 pixels resizes the drawing buffer to match.
- A new `SessionFeed` updates animals without replacing the scene or allocating
  another GPU device.
- Three App unmounts remove the canvas and development reference, stop render
  calls and the animation loop, dispose scene geometry and materials, and reset
  engine resource counts.
- Every device created by three StrictMode mounts receives exactly one native
  `destroy()` call and resolve `device.lost` with reason `destroyed`.
- One `POST /rpc` stays alive across those mounts through the page's feed consumer.

The run enables WebGPU in headless Chrome and permits a SwiftShader fallback.
The lifecycle check proves actual habitat teardown, not driver-memory recovery,
responsive layout, accessibility, pixel comparison, or visual acceptance.

## Interaction and specimen coverage

The habitat smoke now verifies one mobile overlay invariant at 390x844:
placard open, title focus, and clipboard confirmation leave the canvas bounds,
drawing buffer, and camera matrices unchanged. It also checks Escape focus
return and outside close. This is bounded interaction coverage, not complete
responsive or accessibility acceptance. Real pointer ray hits and keyboard
focus are exercised by `interaction`; `scene` checks camera aspect after CSS
resize, and `specimen` changes DPR without changing CSS size. The specimen
camera renders independently, so its downsampled appearance and pose are compared
with the board rather than requiring identical pixels.

## Still unverified

- Shader, lighting, material, and density acceptance for the production scene,
  and a pixel-level comparison against the approved Kreisel.
- Supersampling and an accepted performance baseline on a named device, browser,
  viewport, pixel ratio, and rendering protocol. One five-minute live-feed run
  on 11 November 2026 measured SPS and FPS at 60 with flat three.js resource
  counts, but it is single-machine evidence, not an accepted baseline.
- A frame-level WebGPU capture. A WebGPU canvas has no `drawingBufferWidth` or
  `drawingBufferHeight`; the habitat smoke reads backend, draw calls, triangles,
  animal counts and poses from the live renderer instead.

## Limits

A canvas element in the page is not proof of rendering. The probe reads draw
calls and buffer dimensions from the live renderer, so it fails when the context
or frame loop is missing. Controlled fixtures, frozen poses, and captured frames
provide bounded regression checks, not approved visual baselines. Driver-memory
recovery and long-run performance still require measurements outside this smoke.
